## Choose a practice route

**Grade 6 · After Thinking Together or A Decision We Can Explain · With a teacher and a partner**

Use this pack when you want more practice explaining, responding and using feedback. There are six routes. **Choose one route with your teacher.** You do not need to do them all.

**Feeling like a lot?** Start with route 2, the shortest. In any route, choose one fact, say one reason, and answer one thing your partner says. That is a complete start.

Keep **Case Sheet: The Reading-Corner Decision** open for the facts and prices. For words to start with, open **Sentence Starters for Thinking Together**; your own words are welcome too.

### 1. Try a clearer exchange (about 15 minutes)

Use **Practice Record: Try, Notice, Retry**: get a message ready → your partner replies → you respond → ask for one piece of feedback → try again → compare your two tries. **Pause and Try: Choose a Move** has picture-supported examples. **Repair the Exchange** is a written alternative with teacher feedback.

### 2. Read a discussion record (about 10 minutes)

Open **Read the Record: Reply or Group Plan?** For each record, ask: Does someone reply to what another person meant? Does the group agree on a plan? Sort it as a reply, a group plan, both, or neither, using the words in the record. Before you press **Check**, explain one choice; then open **Why?** to compare. Placements reset when you close the sort, so write one note in the last row of the Practice Record if you want to keep it.

### 3. Picture versus record (about 12 minutes)

Use **Picture, Record, Reconsider** with **Evidence Investigator’s Notebook**. Describe something in a picture, compare it with the written record, and ask a question. Judge what the record shows, not how people look.

### 4. Design a group routine (about 30–40 minutes)

Compare **Two Ways to Organize Our Thinking**, then use **Design, Test, and Revise Our Routine** to try one and decide what to keep.

### 5. Try the moves in science (about 20 minutes)

**Transfer Lab: What Should We Test Next?** uses new paper-bridge data and **Next Round: My Learning Record**.

### 6. Bring your own decision (about 30 minutes)

Use **Bring Your Own Decision** to try the same moves on a real decision your class faces, with your teacher’s help.

Use speech, writing, typing, signing, a communication board or device (AAC), or a labeled sketch. Keep the tools and thinking time you need.

**Credit:** Adapted from ideas in Katie Novak’s article [“Beyond Turn & Talk: How to Teach Academic Discourse and Collaboration”](https://www.novakeducation.com/blog/how-to-teach-academic-discourse-and-collaboration) (Novak Education, 2026). These are original AlloFlow activities; Katie Novak did not write or endorse them.

## Case Sheet: The Reading-Corner Decision

**Use with every activity in this pack.** Keep this sheet open while you work.

### The fictional case

Recommend equipment and a routine for a school reading corner. Spend **at most 6 equipment tokens**. All facts and prices are invented. A teacher must check furniture fit and shelf access before any real change.

**Evidence A: Preferences.** In a fictional class of 30, 24 selected a quiet place for independent reading and 18 selected a place to discuss a book with a partner. They could select both choices, so do not add the counts to find a class total.

**Evidence B: A space check.** In the trial layout, a large fixed table blocked the route to one shelf. Any new plan must keep a clear route to every shelf. The teacher will check the actual layout before use.

**Evidence C: A sound check.** During three practice sessions, partner talk could be heard across this small corner. No one has tested whether a divider would reduce that sound.

**Evidence D: A light check.** The existing corner light does not reach every reading position. The room already has another well-lit reading area.

**Evidence E: Available equipment.** A divider costs 3 tokens; a task lamp costs 2; a movable table costs 3; a book basket costs 1; a set of seat pads costs 2. Choose each item at most once. A divider can mark two areas but is not guaranteed to block sound. A movable table can be repositioned; its fit must be checked. A basket can bring books closer; it must not block the route. Seat pads add floor-seating choices, but floor seating is optional. A lamp adds light at one position; check cords and placement before use.

### Two ideas to start with

- **Plan 1:** a lamp (2) and book basket (1): **3 tokens**. Add a schedule for quiet reading and partner discussion. This adds light at one position; it does not light every seat.
- **Plan 2:** a divider (3) and book basket (1): **4 tokens**. Add the same schedule. This marks two areas; it does not prove that sound is blocked.

Compare these starting ideas. You may keep or change them within the budget. If you agree immediately, compare your reasons and one concern.

### Check your own work

- I can explain my idea with a case fact and a reason.
- I can respond to what my partner meant, and use one piece of feedback to try again.
- I can help make a shared recommendation and name one thing we still need to check.

**Credit:** Adapted from ideas in Katie Novak’s article [“Beyond Turn & Talk: How to Teach Academic Discourse and Collaboration”](https://www.novakeducation.com/blog/how-to-teach-academic-discourse-and-collaboration) (Novak Education, 2026). This is an original AlloFlow case sheet; Katie Novak did not write or endorse it.

cues.guidance: Use this record with a discussion topic and information you and your partner can both access. Name your topic and choose one goal for this practice, such as explaining a reason or checking meaning. Use rows 1–5; row 6 belongs to the separate record sort. If helpful, borrow one cue from Sentence Starters for Thinking Together or use your own wording. Keep familiar communication tools and thinking time.

Write your first message → your partner’s real reply → your response. Check together that the notes say what each person meant. Brief notes are enough. If no reply has arrived, record “still waiting” and arrange a chance to continue.
Ask a partner or educator for one observation and one action you can try. Record feedback about your actual attempt. The optional feedback picture models this step; it is not your exchange.
Try the feedback action and receive a new reply. Record what each person communicated; keep the first attempt above. You may keep, revise, or question the proposal with a reason.

Compare the attempts. Point to something clearer, a useful idea from your partner, or a remaining question. Name one thing to keep or try next; a needed opportunity is a valid next step. Summary and Connections are optional. You can keep the whole record in your usual format.

Only for Read the Record: Reply or Group Plan? Keep one excerpt, your category, the supporting words, and what remains unknown. Save this note while the sort is open: placements reset when you leave. Use this row or your usual format; there is no need to explain all eight cards.

panels.caption:
**Picture:** Two learners with a tablet, a notebook and separate papers.

**The moment:** One person is still getting their message ready. Another asks, “Are we ready to choose?”

**Your job:** Help the group hear everyone before deciding. You could ask what the person needs, offer a different way to share, or suggest more time. More than one move can work.

**Try it:** Get your own message ready. Your partner answers in their own way. Respond to what they meant. If they have not answered yet, that does not mean they agree.

**Write it down:** In **Practice Record: Try, Notice, Retry**, fill in **Topic + goal**, **First attempt**, **One feedback point**, **Retry** and **What changed or remains uncertain?**

panels.title: Keep a proposal—with reasons
panels.caption:
**The situation:** Partner 1 wants a lamp and basket (3 tokens): some reading spots are dark, and a basket brings books closer. Partner 2 wants a divider and basket (4 tokens): the class wants both quiet reading and partner talk, and a divider can mark two areas. The room has another well-lit reading area. Nobody has tested whether a divider blocks sound.

**Partner 1 could keep the plan:** “You want separate areas for quiet reading and partner talk. I still choose the lamp and basket, because some reading spots here are dark and a lamp can light one of them. Your idea makes me ask how we will fit in both kinds of reading. Nobody has tested the sound yet, and we still need to check the cord, where things go, and the paths to the shelves. What have I missed?”

**Compare both replies:** In each one, find (1) the partner’s idea it answers, (2) a case fact and why it matters, and (3) something still to check. Both replies are reasonable; neither is the one right answer.

**Your turn:** In your own words, keep, change or question a plan, and give a reason. Then answer your partner’s real reply in **Practice Record: Try, Notice, Retry**. If no reply has come yet, write “still waiting.”

history.title: Repair the Exchange
history.meta: Optional analysis of fictional messages | Four short questions complete the activity; both reflections are optional | Teacher feedback

questions.question: Use the facts and prices in Case Sheet: The Reading-Corner Decision. A message says: “The divider will make the corner silent. Buy it.” Another says: “I’m thinking about a task lamp because some reading spots are too dark.” The first reply is: “That does not matter.” Write a better next message in your own words. It should (1) respond to the lamp idea and (2) check the divider claim against the case. Then explain how your message helps the pair compare plans.
questions.expectedAnswer: Accept multiple repairs. Look for an accurate response to the lighting proposal, a request to clarify or compare it, and recognition that the divider’s sound effect has not been tested. The case describes uneven lighting; one lamp does not solve every position. For example, a response could check whether the partner wants a lamp at one location and ask how both plans address the case. A polite phrase alone, or substituting a preferred purchase without responding to the other idea, is incomplete. Coach the missing move, not the exact wording. Do not grade speech fluency, grammar unrelated to meaning, or use of a communication support.

questions.question: A group member types a question: “Before we choose the movable table, how will we check the path to every shelf?” The recorder answers, “We already had our turns,” and ends the discussion. Name two things the group could do now: (1) answer the question, and (2) let the person who asked check that the group understood it. How could this change the plan?
questions.expectedAnswer: A strong response takes the route question seriously, links it to the blocked shelf route or the need to check the movable table’s fit, and reopens the comparison or records a check needed before use. It also provides response time and a way for the contributor to confirm or correct the group’s interpretation through a workable communication method. Merely granting another turn without using the message, reading it aloud without checking its meaning, or requiring speech is insufficient. A written, typed, signed, AAC, spoken, or labeled-sketch exchange may satisfy the same criteria.

questions.question: Open Pause and Try: Choose a Move and read the two replies, “Keep a proposal—with reasons” and “Revise a proposal—with reasons.” The pictures are optional. For each reply, find (1) the partner’s idea it answers, (2) a case fact and the reason it matters, and (3) something still to check.

brief.context:
Your group is about to compare plans for the reading corner again. Plan how you will share, check and use everyone’s ideas before deciding. Option A — respond as you go: Everyone gets ready first. One person shares an idea. Check that you understood it, then answer its reason or question. Do the same for the next idea. Then compare the ideas together and agree on a next step, or write down a concern that is still open.

Option B — collect, confirm, then compare: Everyone gets ready first. Collect all the ideas in one shared record that everyone can use. Each person checks that the record says what they meant, and fixes it if not. Then compare the ideas and answer their reasons or questions together. Agree on a next step, or write down a concern that is still open.

Both are good starting points. You may combine or change them, as long as everyone still gets ready, answers each other and decides together. Choose one thing about how your group works that you want to test. Leave out names and personal details.

lockedLessonFacts: Academic discourse means talking to learn: sharing ideas, explaining reasons, asking questions, thinking about other views, and answering others' thinking.
Collaboration means joining everyone’s ideas toward a shared goal: sharing jobs, deciding together, and solving problems. A finished product alone does not show how people worked together.
Time to get ready, sentence starters you can see, different ways to communicate, and enough time to answer help everyone take part. Partners need ways to take in and answer each other’s ideas.
Students can help make the group’s rules, practice ways of working together, and look back on ideas and decisions to choose a next step.

## Try the moves in a new subject

**Optional science-and-data route: about 20 minutes.** This task has its own facts and goal. All the numbers are made up for practice. You do not need to build a bridge.

### The bridge team's decision

A class tested two folded-paper bridge designs. Before choosing one to show at a demonstration, it can test one design three more times.

**Your shared goal:** Recommend which design to investigate next, explain what you want to find out, and describe how to make the repeated trials useful.

### Bridge evidence

- **Design A:** supported 12, 13, and 12 identical paper clips in its three trials.
- **Design B:** supported 16, 8, and 17 identical paper clips in its three trials.
- **How they tested:** same paper and sheet size, same gap between supports, same kind of clip, and a new bridge for each trial. Each design used its own folds. Clips were added one at a time at the center, waiting 10 seconds after each one. The load is the most clips the bridge held for 10 seconds before the next clip made it fall.
- **What is missing:** the record does not say why the results varied. Three trials cannot tell us what will happen every time. More trials add evidence, but repeating a test does not explain a cause on its own.

**Optional picture support:** **Bridge Lab: Choose a Useful Question** shows the six results and compares two questions. Its caption has everything, so the picture is optional. Then come back here.

### Prepare, compare, decide

1. **Prepare (3 minutes).** Study both sets of results. Compare two questions: Why did the results vary? If we test our design three more times the same way, how many clips will it hold? Which question can three more trials answer, and which can they not answer? Choose Design A or B and a next question, in your own words if you like. Find two numbers or test details that support your thinking. Get your idea ready in a way that works for you.
2. **Exchange (6 minutes).** Explain your idea. Check that you understood someone else’s idea, then answer its reason. If everyone chose the same design, compare your reasons or questions. For sentence starters, use **Sentence Starters for Thinking Together**, or your own words. Keep this round’s work in **Next Round: My Learning Record**.
3. **Decide together (6 minutes).** In **Our decision and exchange** in **Next Round: My Learning Record**, write one recommendation. Include the design to test next and two numbers or details that support it. Add your question, what to keep the same, and one thing the record cannot tell you yet. Say how three more trials could help with your question, and what would still be unknown. Say how someone else’s idea changed your thinking, or why you kept your idea after thinking about it. Write down any concern that is still open.
4. **Check your learning (5 minutes).** Use the record guide below. Point to one real exchange and what it changed, or name a next step if you do not have that yet. Take more time to prepare or communicate if you need it.

Your group can use writing, a labeled sketch, speech, signing, a communication board or device (AAC), or another way that works. One person can record, or each person keeps a copy; check that it says what each person meant. Each person reflects on their own part as well as the group’s decision.

### Make a record you can use

Use **Next Round: My Learning Record**. Keep earlier entries and label new notes by activity or round.

- **My next move:** Choose one action you want to try before the exchange.
- **Our routine:** Record how the group will receive ideas and reach a decision.
- **Our decision and exchange:** Keep the recommendation from step 3, then one real message, the reply, and what it changed. Short notes are enough. Check that you wrote what people meant; no names are needed.
- **Support choice:** Name what helped and what you will keep or change. Needed communication and access supports remain available.

In **Summary**, finish two short checks:

- “My learning: I can point to ___ / I need another try at ___.”
- “Our group’s learning: Our decision shows ___ / Our next action is ___.”

You can write “not yet observed.” If you did not get a real chance to take part, name what got in the way and one change the group could make. You do not have to claim improvement you cannot show.

## Bring Your Own Decision

**Route 6 · About 30 minutes · With a partner or small group**

Use the same discussion moves on a real decision your class faces. Your teacher helps you choose one.

### Pick a decision

Choose a decision that is real, small and safe to talk about, such as how to organize the class library, which game to play at indoor recess, or how to set up a class event. Your teacher checks the choice, and may offer a few to pick from. Leave out names and personal details about anyone.

### 1. Agree on the goal

Write one sentence that says what a good decision would do, such as “Everyone can find a book quickly.” Agree on one rule for how you will work together.

### 2. Gather facts

List three to five facts you know, and one thing you would need to find out. Facts can come from things you have noticed, a quick class poll your teacher approves, or information your teacher gives you.

### 3. Prepare (1–2 minutes)

On your own, choose an idea, one fact and a reason. You can use: **“I propose ____. The fact that ____ matters because ____.”**

### 4. Exchange ideas

Explain your idea. Check what your partner meant: **“Do you mean ____?”** Then answer their reason. Swap who starts. Wait until each person is done before you answer.

### 5. Get feedback and try again

Ask your partner or teacher for one thing that would make your reason or reply clearer. Try it, and answer the new reply. Keep your first try too.

### 6. Decide together

Write your recommendation, two facts with reasons, and one thing that still needs checking. If you still disagree, write down both ideas and how you could test them.

### 7. Reflect

What helped you decide together? What would you change next time? Your teacher will tell you what happens next, for example sharing it with the class or trying it for a week.

Keep your work in **Practice Record: Try, Notice, Retry**. Its rows fit your first try, one piece of feedback, your second try and what changed. Any other format that works for you is fine too. Use speech, writing, typing, signing, a communication board or device (AAC), or a labeled sketch.

data.hook:
## Choose one route by need

Use this pack after **Thinking Together** or **A Decision We Can Explain**. It is a menu, not a checklist: choose one route that fits what you saw. Route 2 is the lightest place to start.

1. **Try a clearer exchange** (about 15 minutes): **Practice Record: Try, Notice, Retry** with the **Pause and Try** examples; **Repair the Exchange** is a written alternative.
2. **Read a discussion record** (about 10 minutes): **Read the Record: Reply or Group Plan?** Ask for one placement explained with exact words, then use **Why?** after Check.
3. **Picture versus record** (about 12 minutes): **Picture, Record, Reconsider** with the **Evidence Investigator’s Notebook**. The written records supply the exchanges; appearance alone cannot show reasoning.
4. **Design a group routine** (about 30–40 minutes): **Two Ways to Organize Our Thinking**, then **Design, Test, and Revise Our Routine**.
5. **Try the moves in science** (about 20 minutes): **Transfer Lab** with **Bridge Lab** and **Next Round: My Learning Record**. Either design can be chosen with reasons; more trials add load data but cannot alone explain why results varied.
6. **Bring your own decision** (about 30 minutes): **Bring Your Own Decision**, kept in the **Practice Record**. Approve the decision first; keep it small, real and free of names or personal details. Prepare three to five facts and two backup decisions in advance, so groups can start quickly. You decide what happens to a recommendation; tell learners what that will be.
data.directInstruction:
## Keep the same goal

Every route keeps the core goal: a reason linked to evidence, and a real response to another person’s idea. Keep needed communication tools, reading supports and thinking time. A missing reply needs another opportunity, not an invented one; learners record “still waiting.”

Sentence starters can fade as learners grow more confident with the moves: whole starters, then first words, then their own wording. Access supports stay.
data.guidedPractice:
## Sort reference

Records 1–2: a reply only. Records 3–4: a group plan only. Records 5–6: both. Records 7–8: neither. The explanations under **Why?** point to the supporting words. Private preparation can be useful; a planned exchange is not an observed reply, and an agreed plan does not show that it happened.
data.independentPractice:
## What to look for

- **Rehearsal:** a first attempt, one feedback point, a retry, and an honest note on what changed.
- **Records and pictures:** the learner points to exact words, and separates what is recorded from what is guessed.
- **Routine:** one step kept or changed, with a reason from an actual trial.
- **Transfer:** two numbers or test details with reasons, a question the next trials can answer, and one uncertainty.
- **Own decision:** a goal sentence, two facts with reasons, one feedback point and a retry, and one thing still to check.

successCriteria: I can keep a first try, one piece of feedback and a second try.

I can use the same discussion moves in a new subject and say what helped.
